segments.text: American Foresters vowed to extinguish every wildfire by 10 a.m. the next day and spent a
century building the fuel load for megafires. This is unintended consequences, episode 84.
On a late August morning in 1910, smoke from the Big Burn still hung over the northern
Rockies, as crews counted the dead. The U.S. Forest Service responded by declaring that
no fire should ever again be allowed to escape initial attack. The policy that followed
treated wildfire as an industrial problem that could be solved with enough men, shovels,
and aircraft. It worked for a while, until the forests themselves began to change. The men who
shaped the 10 a.m. policy were not ideologues. They were professional foresters trained in European
silver culture and shaken by the 1910 fires that killed 87 people and blackened 3 million acres
in two days. Ferdinand Silcox, who became Chief of the Forest Service in 1933, formalized the
goal in 1935. Every fire reported would be controlled by 10 a.m. the following day. The logic was
straightforward. Young timber plantations represented decades of public investment. Towns and
ranches sat in the path of flames. The technology of the era, lookouts, roads, and seasonal crews,
made rapid attacks seem both feasible and responsible. At the same time, federal managers viewed
indigenous burning practices as careless or primitive. Those practices had maintained
open ponderosa stands and reduced understory fuels for centuries. Suppressing both the fires
and the people who set them appeared in the 1930s and 1940s as simple progress. A single mature
ponderosa pine could yield thousands of bored feet of lumber after 40 or 50 years of growth.
Losing it to fire meant writing off the payroll, the planting crews, and the road building costs
already sunk into that stand. European models of sustained yield forestry assumed that removing
fire would let managers schedule harvests the way a factory schedule shifts. The 10 a.m. rule was
written into forest service manuals and enforced through budgets that rewarded quick containment.
Smokey Bear arrived in 1944 as the public face of the campaign. His slogan,
only you can prevent forest fires, reach school rooms, and billboards across the west.
By the 1950s, the agency could point to measurable success. The average annual area burned in
the lower 48 states had dropped from roughly 30 million acres in the early 20th century to fewer
than 5 million. When the 1961 interagency fire plan reinforced the same target, even skeptics
inside the agency accepted that the policy had protected timber and saved lives. A few range
scientists and ecologists noted that some forests now carried heavier fuel loads. Their reports
stayed in technical journals while the political and budgetary incentives remained firmly on the
side of total suppression. Lookout towers were spaced so that any smoke column could be triangulated
within minutes. New roads let engines reach the fire line before noon. The civilian conservation
core and later the military surplus aircraft turned seasonal firefighting into a standing industrial
capacity. Decade after decade of successful extinguishment allowed shade tolerant furs and dense
thickets to fill once open stands. In the Sierra Nevada and the northern Rockies, canopy closure
increased and ladder fuels climbed toward the crowns. When lightning finally found a dry August,
the accumulated biomass produced fires that no initial attack force could contain.
The 1988 Yellowstone fires burned more than 1.3 million acres inside the park,
despite the largest mobilization in agency history. Subsequent events, the 2002 biscuit fire,
the 2013 rimfire, the 2020 August complex, repeated the pattern at larger scales.
Each suppression dollar spent in the short run deferred and magnified the eventual cost. By the 2010s,
the forest service was spending more than half its budget on firefighting rather than on management.
The second order effect reached communities. Denser forests meant hotter fires that crossed
containment lines and destroyed homes built during the decades when the landscape had appeared
stable. Indigenous knowledge of frequent low intensity burning had been actively criminalized.
Its absence removed the only process that had once kept fuels in check. In a typical pre-suppression
ponderosa pine stand, surface fires every five to 15 years consumed needles and killed small
seedlings, while leaving the thick barked adults untouched. Without those fires, seedlings of
Douglas fir and white fir survived in the shade. They grew into pole-sized trees and created
continuous vertical fuel from the forest floor to the canopy. A fire that once moved at a few
chains per hour through grass now carried flames through interlocking crowns at rates measured in
miles per day. By the late 1970s, the forest service began experimenting with let-burn zones in
remote wilderness areas. The 1995 federal wildland fire management policy formally recognized fire
as a natural process. Prescribed burning expanded, yet the acreage treated each year remains far
below the millions of hectares that once burned under Indigenous stewardship. Small
regulations, liability fears, and narrow-burn windows limited operations. Decades of fuel accumulation
made some prescribed fires themselves risky. Today, the agency and its partners treat roughly
three to four million acres annually with fire or mechanical thinning. That figure is still
an order of magnitude short of historical norms. Costs continue to rise. The 2020 fire season alone
exceeded two billion dollars in federal suppression spending. Even the shift toward managed fire
has encountered limits set by the altered landscape itself. A prescribed burn in a stand that now
holds three or four times the historical fuel load can escape under the same weather conditions
that once produced only a light surface fire. Mechanical thinning removes biomass but leaves
slash that must be burned or hauled away. Removing or recurring natural disturbance does not eliminate
disturbance. It concentrates the energy for rarer, larger events. Incentive structures that reward
immediate visible containment will reliably underfund the slower work of restoring process.
When a management regime succeeds at scale, the very success changes the system it was designed
to protect. The original rule set eventually stops describing reality. The practical question for
any complex system is therefore not whether disturbance will occur but whether the rules in place
will let it occur at a scale the landscape and the people on it can absorb. Consider the same
pattern in modern financial regulation where repeated bailouts and circuit breakers reduce small
failures yet steadily build the conditions for the next systemic shock. What early warning signs
in those systems are being sidelined by the same short term incentives that once favored total
fire suppression. We'll leave it there for today. Thanks for thinking through this one with me.
